questions.unit: Unit 2: Probability, Random Variables, and Probability Distributions
questions.prompt: On a wildlife reserve, a trail camera records a fox on 28% of nights, a coyote on 19% of nights, and at least one of the two animals on 39% of nights. What is the probability that the camera records both a fox and a coyote on a randomly selected night?
questions.explanation: P(fox ∪ coyote) = P(fox) + P(coyote) − P(both). Therefore P(both) = 0.28 + 0.19 − 0.39 = 0.08.

questions.unit: Unit 1: Exploring One-Variable Data and Collecting Data
questions.prompt: A high school has a numbered roster of 1,840 students. The principal wants a simple random sample of 60 students for a survey about locker access. Which procedure produces a simple random sample?

choices.A: Use a random-number generator to select 60 distinct roster numbers from 1 through 1,840.
choices.B: Randomly select 3 homerooms and survey the first 20 students entering each room.
choices.C: Survey every 30th student on the roster, beginning with student number 30.
choices.D: Invite all students to respond and use the first 60 completed surveys.

questions.correctAnswerText: Use a random-number generator to select 60 distinct roster numbers from 1 through 1,840.
questions.explanation: Selecting 60 distinct roster numbers at random gives every possible group of 60 students an equal chance of selection. The alternatives introduce clustering, a fixed systematic start, or voluntary response.

questions.unit: Unit 4: Inference for Quantitative Data: Means
questions.prompt: An acoustics engineer tests H0: μ = 1.20 seconds against Ha: μ < 1.20 seconds, where μ is the population mean echo time in rooms fitted with a new wall panel. The test gives a p-value of 0.018. Which interpretation of the p-value is correct?

choices.A: There is a 1.8% probability that the population mean echo time equals 1.20 seconds.
choices.B: About 1.8% of fitted rooms have echo times below the sample mean.
choices.C: If the new panel truly produces a mean echo time below 1.20 seconds, the probability of the observed result is 0.018.
choices.D: If the population mean is 1.20 seconds, the probability of obtaining a sample mean at least as low as the observed one is 0.018.

questions.correctAnswerText: If the population mean is 1.20 seconds, the probability of obtaining a sample mean at least as low as the observed one is 0.018.
questions.explanation: A p-value is computed under H0 and measures the probability of a test statistic at least as extreme in the direction of Ha. It is not the probability that H0 is true.

questions.unit: Unit 5: Regression Analysis
questions.prompt: A scatterplot of elevation gain and water consumed for 22 day hikes has a positive linear pattern with r = 0.62. One hike has much greater elevation gain than all the others. When that hike is removed, r becomes 0.81. Which statement is best supported?

choices.A: The unusual hike strengthened the positive linear association and was not influential.
choices.B: The unusual hike weakened the measured linear association and was influential with respect to r.
choices.C: Removing the hike proves that greater elevation gain causes greater water consumption.
choices.D: The unusual hike must have had a residual of zero because its x-value was extreme.

questions.correctAnswerText: The unusual hike weakened the measured linear association and was influential with respect to r.
questions.explanation: Removing the point raises r from 0.62 to 0.81, so the point had substantially weakened the measured linear association. The large change shows influence on r, but it does not establish causation or determine the residual.

questions.unit: Unit 3: Inference for Categorical Data: Proportions
questions.prompt: A technician plans a one-proportion z-test of H0: p = 0.10 using a random sample of 80 network routers from a population of 5,000 routers. Which condition for the normal approximation is not satisfied under H0?

choices.A: The sample was selected at random.
choices.B: The expected number of routers with the characteristic is at least 10.
choices.C: The expected number of routers without the characteristic is at least 10.
choices.D: The sample size is less than 10% of the population size.

questions.correctAnswerText: The expected number of routers with the characteristic is at least 10.
questions.explanation: Under H0, the expected counts are np0 = 80(0.10) = 8 and n(1 − p0) = 72. Because 8 < 10, the large-count condition for routers with the characteristic is not satisfied.

questions.unit: Unit 1: Exploring One-Variable Data and Collecting Data
questions.prompt:
The table shows platform dwell times for 18 trains.

Dwell time (minutes)       2    3    4    5    8
Number of trains           2    5    6    4    1

What is the mean dwell time for these trains?

choices.A: 3.50 minutes
choices.B: 4.00 minutes
choices.C: 4.40 minutes
choices.D: 3.94 minutes

questions.correctAnswerText: 3.94 minutes
questions.explanation: The weighted total is 2(2) + 3(5) + 4(6) + 5(4) + 8(1) = 71 minutes. Dividing by 18 trains gives x̄ = 71/18 ≈ 3.94 minutes.

questions.unit: Unit 2: Probability, Random Variables, and Probability Distributions
questions.prompt: An online course awards a distinction to each participant independently with probability 0.35. A researcher wants to simulate the probability that at most 2 of 12 participants earn a distinction. Which simulation design is appropriate?

choices.A: Let two-digit numbers 00–34 represent a distinction and 35–99 represent no distinction; generate 12 independent numbers per trial and record whether at most 2 represent distinctions.
choices.B: Let digits 0–2 represent a distinction and 3–9 represent no distinction; generate 12 digits per trial and record whether exactly 2 represent distinctions.
choices.C: Generate one number from 00–99 per trial and count the trial as a success if the number is 00–34.
choices.D: Shuffle 12 cards, 2 labeled distinction and 10 labeled no distinction, and draw all cards per trial.

questions.correctAnswerText: Let two-digit numbers 00–34 represent a distinction and 35–99 represent no distinction; generate 12 independent numbers per trial and record whether at most 2 represent distinctions.
questions.explanation: Thirty-five of 100 equally likely labels model probability 0.35, 12 generated values model the 12 independent participants, and counting trials with 0, 1, or 2 distinctions models “at most 2.”

questions.unit: Unit 3: Inference for Categorical Data: Proportions
questions.prompt: An environmental agency tests H0: p = 0.06 against Ha: p > 0.06, where p is the proportion of private wells in a county with contaminant levels above a safety limit. Which situation describes a Type II error?

choices.A: The agency concludes that p > 0.06 when the true value is 0.06.
choices.B: The agency concludes that p < 0.06 when the true value is 0.06.
choices.C: The agency fails to conclude that p > 0.06 when the true value is 0.09.
choices.D: The agency fails to conclude that p > 0.06 when the true value is 0.06.

questions.correctAnswerText: The agency fails to conclude that p > 0.06 when the true value is 0.09.
questions.explanation: A Type II error is failing to reject H0 when the alternative is true. Here the agency misses a genuinely elevated well-contamination proportion.

questions.unit: Unit 1: Exploring One-Variable Data and Collecting Data
questions.prompt: In a randomized experiment, 150 adults with seasonal allergies receive either a probiotic capsule or an identical-looking placebo. Neither the participants nor the staff members who rate symptom severity know which treatment each participant receives. What is the main purpose of this double-blind procedure?

choices.A: To reduce placebo effects and observer bias that could systematically affect symptom ratings
choices.B: To guarantee that the treatment groups have exactly the same symptom severity before treatment
choices.C: To make the participants a representative random sample of all adults with allergies
choices.D: To remove natural person-to-person variation from the response variable

questions.correctAnswerText: To reduce placebo effects and observer bias that could systematically affect symptom ratings
questions.explanation: Blinding participants limits response changes caused by knowing the treatment, and blinding evaluators limits differential symptom ratings. It does not create representative sampling or eliminate natural variation.

questions.unit: Unit 4: Inference for Quantitative Data: Means
questions.prompt: A random sample of 16 adults completed a visual puzzle in a mean time of x̄ = 72.4 seconds with s = 8.0 seconds. The sample distribution is approximately symmetric with no outliers. For a 95% confidence interval with df = 15, use t* = 2.131. Which interval estimates the population mean completion time?
questions.explanation: SE = s/√n = 8/4 = 2 seconds, so the margin of error is 2.131(2) = 4.262 seconds. The interval is 72.4 ± 4.262 = (68.138, 76.662), or approximately (68.1, 76.7) seconds.

questions.unit: Unit 4: Inference for Quantitative Data: Means
questions.prompt: Independent random samples of polymer strips made with formulation A and formulation B are tested for tensile strength. The two population standard deviations are unknown. Which procedure is appropriate for estimating the difference in population mean tensile strength, μ_A − μ_B?

choices.A: A one-proportion z-interval
choices.B: A two-sample t-interval for a difference in means
choices.C: A paired t-interval for a mean difference
choices.D: A one-sample t-interval applied to all strips combined

questions.correctAnswerText: A two-sample t-interval for a difference in means
questions.explanation: The response is quantitative, the samples are independent, and the two unknown population means are being compared. Pairing is not present, and a proportion procedure is inappropriate.

questions.unit: Unit 2: Probability, Random Variables, and Probability Distributions
questions.prompt:
Questions APSTAT-MCQ2-012 through APSTAT-MCQ2-014 use the following stimulus. In a university media archive, 60% of stored files are audio and 40% are video. A stored audio file has probability 0.03 of being corrupted, and a stored video file has probability 0.08 of being corrupted.

What is the probability that a randomly selected stored file is corrupted?
questions.explanation: Apply the total-probability rule: P(corrupted) = 0.60(0.03) + 0.40(0.08) = 0.018 + 0.032 = 0.050.

questions.unit: Unit 2: Probability, Random Variables, and Probability Distributions
questions.prompt:
Questions APSTAT-MCQ2-012 through APSTAT-MCQ2-014 use the following stimulus. In a university media archive, 60% of stored files are audio and 40% are video. A stored audio file has probability 0.03 of being corrupted, and a stored video file has probability 0.08 of being corrupted.

Given that a randomly selected file is corrupted, what is the probability that it is a video file?
questions.explanation: P(video and corrupted) = 0.40(0.08) = 0.032. Therefore P(video | corrupted) = 0.032/0.050 = 0.64.

questions.unit: Unit 2: Probability, Random Variables, and Probability Distributions
questions.prompt:
Questions APSTAT-MCQ2-012 through APSTAT-MCQ2-014 use the following stimulus. In a university media archive, 60% of stored files are audio and 40% are video. A stored audio file has probability 0.03 of being corrupted, and a stored video file has probability 0.08 of being corrupted.

Are file type and corruption status independent?

choices.A: No, because the probability of corruption differs between audio and video files.
choices.B: No, because 60% of files are audio and only 40% are video.
choices.C: Yes, because the overall probability of corruption is 0.05.
choices.D: Yes, because every file is either audio or video.

questions.correctAnswerText: No, because the probability of corruption differs between audio and video files.
questions.explanation: Independence would require P(corrupted | audio) = P(corrupted | video) = P(corrupted). Instead, 0.03 and 0.08 differ, so file type and corruption status are associated.

questions.unit: Unit 1: Exploring One-Variable Data and Collecting Data
questions.prompt: The useful lifetimes of a model of 3D-printer nozzle are approximately normal with mean 860 hours and standard deviation 75 hours. About what lifetime marks the 90th percentile? Use z = 1.282 for the 90th percentile of the standard normal distribution.

choices.A: 764 hours
choices.B: 875 hours
choices.C: 935 hours
choices.D: 956 hours

questions.correctAnswerText: 956 hours
questions.explanation: Convert the 90th-percentile z-score back to hours: x = μ + zσ = 860 + 1.282(75) = 956.15 hours, approximately 956 hours.

questions.unit: Unit 3: Inference for Categorical Data: Proportions
questions.prompt: A county sends a recreation survey to a simple random sample of 600 households, but only 38% of the selected households respond. Why might an interval calculated from the responses fail to estimate the proportion of all county households that use public parks?

choices.A: The sample size is too large for a one-proportion interval.
choices.B: Responding households may differ systematically from selected households that did not respond.
choices.C: Random sampling prevents the use of a confidence interval when the response rate is below 50%.
choices.D: The interval would describe only the 600 households even if every selected household responded.

questions.correctAnswerText: Responding households may differ systematically from selected households that did not respond.
questions.explanation: A low response rate can create nonresponse bias if park use is related to whether a household responds. The original random selection does not correct systematic differences between respondents and nonrespondents.

questions.unit: Unit 4: Inference for Quantitative Data: Means
questions.prompt: Two independent random samples compare the mean number of days required for two compost mixtures to decompose. For mixture A, n_A = 20, x̄_A = 31 days, and s_A = 4 days. For mixture B, n_B = 18, x̄_B = 35 days, and s_B = 5 days. For H0: μ_A − μ_B = 0, what is the approximate two-sample t statistic?

questions.unit: Unit 1: Exploring One-Variable Data and Collecting Data
questions.prompt: Counts of plastic fragments in 25 beach sections form a right-skewed distribution. Twenty-four counts are between 6 and 39, and one count is 94. If the count of 94 is removed, which change is most likely?

choices.A: The mean increases, while the median and standard deviation both decrease.
choices.B: The mean and median increase, while the standard deviation decreases.
choices.C: The mean decreases, while the median and standard deviation both increase.
choices.D: The mean and standard deviation decrease, while the median changes little or not at all.

questions.correctAnswerText: The mean and standard deviation decrease, while the median changes little or not at all.
questions.explanation: Removing the extreme high value lowers the mean and greatly reduces spread. Because the median depends on middle positions, deleting one extreme value generally changes it little or not at all.

questions.unit: Unit 5: Regression Analysis
questions.prompt: For wind speeds x between 5 and 15 meters per second, the line ŷ = −120 + 48x predicts the electrical output y, in watts, of a small turbine. Which statement about the intercept is most appropriate?

choices.A: At every wind speed, the turbine loses 120 watts before producing electricity.
choices.B: A 1-meter-per-second increase in wind speed is associated with a 120-watt decrease in predicted output.
choices.C: The intercept predicts −120 watts at zero wind speed, but that value is outside the observed x-range and is not practically meaningful.
choices.D: The turbine will begin producing electricity precisely when wind speed reaches 120 meters per second.

questions.correctAnswerText: The intercept predicts −120 watts at zero wind speed, but that value is outside the observed x-range and is not practically meaningful.
questions.explanation: The intercept is the predicted response at x = 0. Since the observed wind speeds begin at 5 meters per second and negative output is not meaningful here, the numerical intercept should not receive a practical interpretation.

questions.unit: Unit 3: Inference for Categorical Data: Proportions
questions.prompt: Researchers test H0: p = 0.12 against Ha: p < 0.12 for the proportion of patients who experience an adverse reaction. The significance level and the true value of p under the alternative are held fixed. What is the likely effect of increasing the sample size?

choices.A: Both the probability of a Type I error and the power decrease.
choices.B: The power increases because the test can more reliably detect the fixed departure from 0.12.
choices.C: The power stays the same because α is unchanged.
choices.D: The probability of a Type I error increases above α.

questions.correctAnswerText: The power increases because the test can more reliably detect the fixed departure from 0.12.
questions.explanation: A larger sample reduces sampling variability, making a fixed alternative value easier to distinguish from the null. With α fixed, the Type I error rate remains α.

questions.unit: Unit 2: Probability, Random Variables, and Probability Distributions
questions.prompt: Suppose each of 250 incoming email messages is independently classified as phishing with probability 0.04. Let X be the number classified as phishing. What are the mean and standard deviation of X?

choices.A: μ_X = 10 and σ_X ≈ 3.10
choices.B: μ_X = 10 and σ_X ≈ 9.60
choices.C: μ_X = 4 and σ_X ≈ 1.96

questions.correctAnswerText: μ_X = 10 and σ_X ≈ 3.10

questions.unit: Unit 1: Exploring One-Variable Data and Collecting Data
questions.prompt: Researchers compare self-reported stress scores of people who commute by electric bicycle with scores of people who commute by car. Participants chose their own commuting method. Even after the groups are similar in age, the e-bike group has a lower mean stress score. Which conclusion is most appropriate?

choices.A: The study shows an association, but variables such as job location or baseline fitness could confound a causal comparison.
choices.B: Electric bicycles caused the lower mean because the two groups were compared using the same stress scale.
choices.C: The lower mean can be generalized to all commuters because participants selected their usual transportation.
choices.D: A causal conclusion is valid as long as both groups contain at least 30 people.

questions.correctAnswerText: The study shows an association, but variables such as job location or baseline fitness could confound a causal comparison.
questions.explanation: Commuting method was not randomly assigned, so preexisting differences can be related to both method and stress. Matching only on age does not eliminate all plausible confounding.

questions.unit: Unit 4: Inference for Quantitative Data: Means
questions.prompt: A food regulator wants to test whether the population mean mass μ of packages labeled 250 grams is less than the labeled amount. Which hypotheses should be used?
questions.explanation: Equality is placed in H0 at the labeled amount. The regulator seeks evidence of underfilling, so Ha is left-tailed.

questions.unit: Unit 3: Inference for Categorical Data: Proportions
questions.prompt: A 95% confidence interval for p_D − p_P, the difference between the population proportions of customers who pay digitally and on paper before the due date, is (−0.09, 0.02). Which conclusion is supported at the 5% significance level?

choices.A: Digital payment produces a significantly lower on-time proportion.
choices.B: Digital payment produces a significantly higher on-time proportion.
choices.C: The interval does not provide statistically significant evidence of a difference because it includes zero.
choices.D: The two population proportions are equal because the interval contains zero.

questions.correctAnswerText: The interval does not provide statistically significant evidence of a difference because it includes zero.
questions.explanation: Zero is a plausible value for p_D − p_P within the 95% interval, so the corresponding two-sided test would fail to reject equality at α = 0.05. This does not prove the proportions are equal.

questions.unit: Unit 1: Exploring One-Variable Data and Collecting Data
questions.prompt: A botanist measures leaf length in two samples. The 40 oak leaves have mean length 12.5 cm, and the 60 maple leaves have mean length 10.5 cm. What is the mean length of all 100 measured leaves?
questions.explanation: The combined mean must weight the group means by their sample sizes: [40(12.5) + 60(10.5)]/100 = (500 + 630)/100 = 11.3 cm.

questions.unit: Unit 5: Regression Analysis
questions.prompt: An aquarium develops a regression model relating age to body length for a species of fish observed between 2 and 12 months of age. Why should the model not be used to predict the length of a 24-month-old fish?

choices.A: Correlation can be calculated only when age is measured in years.
choices.B: A regression line cannot be used to predict a quantitative response.
choices.C: The prediction is interpolation, so it is guaranteed to be too small.
choices.D: The prediction is an extrapolation, and the age-length pattern may change beyond the observed range.

questions.correctAnswerText: The prediction is an extrapolation, and the age-length pattern may change beyond the observed range.
questions.explanation: Twenty-four months is well beyond the observed 2-to-12-month range. A linear trend within the data range need not continue for older fish.

questions.unit: Unit 2: Probability, Random Variables, and Probability Distributions
questions.prompt: A playlist contains 30 songs, 8 marked explicit and 22 not marked explicit. Five distinct songs will be played in random order without replacement. Which simulation best estimates the probability that none of the five songs is marked explicit?

choices.A: Generate five independent random integers from 1 to 30, allowing repeats, and count trials containing only values 9–30.
choices.B: Generate one random integer from 1 to 30 and count the trial as a success if it is between 9 and 30.
choices.C: Randomly shuffle 8 E cards and 22 N cards, examine the first five cards, and count trials containing five N cards.
choices.D: Flip a fair coin five times and count trials with no heads.

questions.correctAnswerText: Randomly shuffle 8 E cards and 22 N cards, examine the first five cards, and count trials containing five N cards.
questions.explanation: Shuffling the 30 cards and examining five models simple random selection without replacement. Allowing repeats would incorrectly model sampling with replacement.

questions.unit: Unit 3: Inference for Categorical Data: Proportions
questions.prompt: A university independently samples applicants who submitted an optional portfolio and applicants who did not. Let p_P and p_N be the respective population proportions who enroll after admission. The university wants to determine whether the enrollment proportions differ. Which hypotheses are appropriate?

choices.A: H0: p_P − p_N = 0; Ha: p_P − p_N ≠ 0
choices.C: H0: p_P − p_N ≠ 0; Ha: p_P − p_N = 0
choices.D: H0: p_P = p_N; Ha: p_P > p_N

questions.correctAnswerText: H0: p_P − p_N = 0; Ha: p_P − p_N ≠ 0
questions.explanation: The hypotheses concern population proportions, not sample statistics. “Differ” calls for a two-sided alternative, with equality in H0.

questions.unit: Unit 1: Exploring One-Variable Data and Collecting Data
questions.prompt:
The weekly numbers of pages printed by six members of each of two office teams are shown.

Team A: 18, 19, 20, 20, 21, 22
Team B: 14, 18, 20, 20, 22, 26

Which comparison is correct?

choices.A: Team A has the larger mean and the larger standard deviation.
choices.B: The teams have the same mean, but Team B has the larger standard deviation.
choices.C: The teams have the same mean and the same standard deviation.
choices.D: Team B has the larger mean, but Team A has the larger standard deviation.

questions.correctAnswerText: The teams have the same mean, but Team B has the larger standard deviation.
questions.explanation: Each team is symmetric around 20, so both means equal 20 pages. Team B's values lie farther from 20, so Team B has the larger standard deviation.

questions.unit: Unit 4: Inference for Quantitative Data: Means
questions.prompt: Independent random samples of two soup recipes are used to estimate μ_N − μ_C, where μ_N is the population mean sodium content for the new recipe and μ_C is the population mean for the current recipe. A 99% confidence interval, in milligrams per serving, is (1.2, 4.8). Which interpretation is appropriate?

choices.A: Ninety-nine percent of servings of the new recipe contain 1.2 to 4.8 milligrams more sodium than servings of the current recipe.
choices.B: The population mean sodium content of the new recipe is estimated to be 1.2 to 4.8 milligrams higher than that of the current recipe.
choices.C: There is a 99% probability that the sample mean difference lies between 1.2 and 4.8 milligrams.
choices.D: The recipes have practically important different sodium contents because the entire interval is positive.

questions.correctAnswerText: The population mean sodium content of the new recipe is estimated to be 1.2 to 4.8 milligrams higher than that of the current recipe.
questions.explanation: The interval estimates μ_N − μ_C, and both endpoints are positive. It concerns a difference in population means, not individual servings, and statistical evidence alone does not establish practical importance.

questions.unit: Unit 2: Probability, Random Variables, and Probability Distributions
questions.prompt: For two events A and B, P(A) = 0.40, P(B) = 0.25, and P(A ∩ B) = 0.10. Which conclusion is correct?

choices.A: A and B are mutually exclusive because P(A ∩ B) is small.
choices.B: A and B are dependent because P(A) + P(B) ≠ 1.
choices.C: A and B are dependent because P(A | B) = 0.40.
choices.D: A and B are independent because P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B).

questions.correctAnswerText: A and B are independent because P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B).
questions.explanation: P(A)P(B) = 0.40(0.25) = 0.10, which equals P(A ∩ B). This equality is a criterion for independence; events with a positive intersection are not mutually exclusive.

questions.unit: Unit 3: Inference for Categorical Data: Proportions
questions.prompt: An electric utility tests H0: p = 0.55 using a random sample of 160 customers, where p is the population proportion enrolled in automatic payment. The sample proportion is p̂ = 0.60. What is the approximate one-proportion z statistic?

questions.unit: Unit 1: Exploring One-Variable Data and Collecting Data
questions.prompt: Biologists estimate the mean mass of songbirds in a forest by setting mist nets next to a feeding station at dawn and weighing captured birds. Which concern most directly limits generalization to all songbirds in the forest?

choices.A: The mass of a captured bird is quantitative rather than categorical.
choices.B: Measuring at dawn makes random assignment impossible.
choices.C: Birds that visit the feeding station and enter the nets may differ from birds that do not.
choices.D: A census is required whenever wildlife can move between locations.

questions.correctAnswerText: Birds that visit the feeding station and enter the nets may differ from birds that do not.
questions.explanation: The capture location and method can underrepresent birds that avoid feeders or nets. The resulting convenience-like sample need not represent all forest songbirds.

questions.unit: Unit 5: Regression Analysis
questions.prompt:
Questions APSTAT-MCQ2-034 through APSTAT-MCQ2-036 use the following stimulus. In a wind-tunnel study of 15 wing models, x is wing angle in degrees and y is lift coefficient. Computer output gives ŷ = 0.420 + 0.065x and r = 0.867.

Which statement correctly interprets the slope of the regression line?

choices.A: Each additional degree of wing angle causes lift coefficient to increase by exactly 0.420.
choices.B: For each increase of 0.065 degree, predicted lift coefficient increases by 1.
choices.C: At a wing angle of 0 degrees, the observed lift coefficient must equal 0.065.
choices.D: For each additional degree of wing angle, predicted lift coefficient increases by 0.065, on average.

questions.correctAnswerText: For each additional degree of wing angle, predicted lift coefficient increases by 0.065, on average.
questions.explanation: A regression slope gives the change in predicted response for a one-unit increase in x. The wording “predicted” and “on average” avoids an unsupported deterministic or causal claim.

questions.unit: Unit 5: Regression Analysis
questions.prompt:
Questions APSTAT-MCQ2-034 through APSTAT-MCQ2-036 use the following stimulus. In a wind-tunnel study of 15 wing models, x is wing angle in degrees and y is lift coefficient. Computer output gives ŷ = 0.420 + 0.065x and r = 0.867.

Another laboratory reports lift index L = 100y instead of lift coefficient y. Which equation predicts lift index from wing angle?
questions.explanation: Because L = 100y, every predicted response is multiplied by 100. Multiplying both the intercept and slope by 100 gives L̂ = 100(0.420 + 0.065x) = 42.0 + 6.5x.

questions.unit: Unit 5: Regression Analysis
questions.prompt:
Questions APSTAT-MCQ2-034 through APSTAT-MCQ2-036 use the following stimulus. In a wind-tunnel study of 15 wing models, x is wing angle in degrees and y is lift coefficient. Computer output gives ŷ = 0.420 + 0.065x and r = 0.867.

If wing angle is converted from degrees to radians, with all converted values obtained by multiplying by the same positive constant, what happens to the correlation?

choices.A: It remains 0.867 because correlation is unchanged by a positive linear rescaling of either variable.
choices.B: It becomes smaller because numerical angles measured in radians are smaller.
choices.C: It becomes 0.867 times the degrees-to-radians conversion factor.
choices.D: It changes to −0.867 because the scale of the explanatory variable changes.

questions.correctAnswerText: It remains 0.867 because correlation is unchanged by a positive linear rescaling of either variable.
questions.explanation: Converting degrees to radians multiplies every x-value by the same positive constant. Correlation measures standardized linear association, so its magnitude and sign remain unchanged.

questions.unit: Unit 4: Inference for Quantitative Data: Means
questions.prompt: A materials laboratory compares mean breaking strength for tiles fired in kiln A and kiln B. Identical unfired tiles are randomly assigned to a kiln, then their breaking strengths are measured. Why is random assignment important?

choices.A: It makes the tested tiles a simple random sample of all tiles ever manufactured.
choices.B: It tends to balance other tile characteristics between kiln groups, supporting a causal comparison of mean breaking strength for the tiles in the experiment.
choices.C: It guarantees that the two sample standard deviations will be equal.
choices.D: It allows the laboratory to ignore the independence of individual tile measurements.

questions.correctAnswerText: It tends to balance other tile characteristics between kiln groups, supporting a causal comparison of mean breaking strength for the tiles in the experiment.
questions.explanation: Random assignment reduces systematic treatment-group differences in other tile characteristics. It supports causal inference for the experimental units but does not create a random sample from a broader population.

questions.unit: Unit 3: Inference for Categorical Data: Proportions
questions.prompt: In a very large randomized study, an app notification increased the completion proportion from 71.4% to 72.0%, with p-value 0.004. Which statement is most appropriate?

choices.A: The result is not statistically significant because the observed increase is less than 1 percentage point.
choices.B: The app has a large practical effect because the p-value is very small.
choices.C: The null hypothesis has probability 0.004 of being true.
choices.D: The result is statistically significant, but whether a 0.6-percentage-point increase is practically important requires separate judgment.

questions.correctAnswerText: The result is statistically significant, but whether a 0.6-percentage-point increase is practically important requires separate judgment.
questions.explanation: The p-value 0.004 is below common significance levels, so the result is statistically significant. Practical importance depends on the size and consequences of the 0.006 increase, not on the p-value alone.

questions.unit: Unit 1: Exploring One-Variable Data and Collecting Data
questions.prompt: A nutrition researcher wants to compare distributions of sodium content across breakfast, lunch, and dinner menu categories. Which variable definitions are appropriate for this question?

choices.A: Sodium content in milligrams as a quantitative variable and meal category as a categorical variable
choices.B: Sodium content in milligrams as a categorical variable and meal category as a quantitative variable
choices.C: Both sodium content and meal category as quantitative variables
choices.D: Both sodium content and meal category as categorical variables

questions.correctAnswerText: Sodium content in milligrams as a quantitative variable and meal category as a categorical variable
questions.explanation: Sodium content is numerical with meaningful arithmetic, while breakfast, lunch, and dinner are group labels. This setup supports comparing a quantitative distribution across categorical groups.

questions.unit: Unit 2: Probability, Random Variables, and Probability Distributions
questions.prompt: Each independently processed customer-support ticket has probability 0.12 of being escalated. None of the first 20 tickets today were escalated. What does the law of large numbers suggest?

choices.A: The next ticket must be escalated so that the proportion begins moving toward 0.12.
choices.B: Exactly 12 of the next 100 tickets will be escalated.
choices.C: Over a very large number of tickets, the overall escalated proportion is likely to approach 0.12, but short runs can vary substantially.
choices.D: The long-run escalation probability has fallen below 0.12 because the first 20 were not escalated.

questions.correctAnswerText: Over a very large number of tickets, the overall escalated proportion is likely to approach 0.12, but short runs can vary substantially.
questions.explanation: The law of large numbers describes long-run relative frequency. Independence means the first 20 outcomes neither force the next outcome nor change its escalation probability.

questions.unit: Unit 3: Inference for Categorical Data: Proportions
questions.prompt: Two 95% confidence intervals are constructed for a population proportion. Both samples have the same value of p̂, but one sample has n = 100 and the other has n = 400. Assuming all conditions are met, how do their approximate margins of error compare?

choices.A: The margin for n = 400 is one-fourth the margin for n = 100.
choices.B: The margin for n = 400 is one-half the margin for n = 100.
choices.C: The margins are equal because p̂ and the confidence level are equal.
choices.D: The margin for n = 400 is twice the margin for n = 100.

questions.correctAnswerText: The margin for n = 400 is one-half the margin for n = 100.
questions.explanation: With p̂ and confidence level fixed, margin of error is proportional to 1/√n. Increasing n by a factor of 4 multiplies the margin by 1/√4 = 1/2.

questions.unit: Unit 1: Exploring One-Variable Data and Collecting Data
questions.prompt: A factory records the defect classification of every item produced during one Tuesday. Which statement best describes the resulting data?

choices.A: They are a simple random sample of all items the factory will ever produce.
choices.B: They permit a causal conclusion about why Tuesday defects occurred.
choices.C: They are a voluntary-response sample because workers chose which items to produce.
choices.D: They are a census of Tuesday's production, but generalizing to production on other days requires additional justification.

questions.correctAnswerText: They are a census of Tuesday's production, but generalizing to production on other days requires additional justification.
questions.explanation: Every item in the defined Tuesday population was recorded, so the data are a census of that day. Tuesday's conditions may differ from other days, so broader generalization is not automatic.
